# Diagnosing Persistent P0306 on the 2002 Jeep Liberty KJ

You've replaced the spark coil, swapped in a known-good unit for cylinder 6, cleaned every injector on the rail, and even gambled on a new camshaft position sensor. The check engine light remains stubbornly fixed at P0306. You're also experiencing that specific "buck" where the engine feels like it's trying to die until you release the throttle or downshift. This isn't just a random miss; it's a load-dependent failure mode that points away from simple component substitution.

On the 2002 Jeep Liberty with the 3.7L V6 (the KR engine), swapping coils is a common first step, but the symptoms you describe suggest we need to look deeper into the ignition control architecture and mechanical integrity of the head. The fact that the vehicle runs "barely drive-able" after sitting implies a fuel pressure issue or an air leak that becomes apparent only under load. However, the persistent P0306 despite multiple coil swaps strongly indicates the problem lies within the coil itself in a way that replacement didn't fix, or the signal path is compromised.

### The Ignition Control Module (ICM) Hypothesis

You asked if these engines have an ignition control module or transistor pack. Yes, the 3.7L V6 utilizes an Ignition Control Module (often referred to as the Transistor Driver Pack) mounted directly on the engine block near the distributor housing or the front of the transmission tunnel, depending on the specific trim and year variation.

The KR engine uses a unique ignition system where the ICM fires the coils based on signals from the crankshaft and camshaft sensors. If the coil pack itself is failing internallyâperhaps due to moisture ingress or degraded internal windingsâit might have functioned when cold but failed immediately upon heating up, which matches your observation of the car buckling after driving a mile up hills. However, since you swapped coils and the code persisted, the ICM is the next logical suspect for a single-cylinder failure.

The ICM can develop an internal short or fail to fire one specific cylinder even if all coils are good. This often happens when the coil wires are damaged or if there is excessive resistance in the firing circuit. When this occurs, the engine will misfire under load because the ECU cannot maintain the spark timing required for combustion at higher RPMs and vacuum loads. The "buck" you feel is the result of unburned fuel entering the exhaust system, which can overheat the catalytic converter if left too long.

### Mechanical Integrity and Vacuum Leaks

Another critical area to investigate is the ignition coil boot and the spark plug wire connection (if equipped) or the direct spark plug tower connection. On these older Jeep Liberties, a cracked rubber boot on the coil tower for cylinder 6 can allow high-voltage current to arc to ground when the engine is hot and expanding. This creates a false misfire code because the ECU detects a lack of primary/secondary circuit integrity, even though the physical component (the coil) was replaced.

Additionally, consider the spark plug itself. If the plug has an internal short or severe carbon tracking on the insulator, it can cause a persistent P0306 regardless of the coil. Ensure you are using the correct gap setting for the specific OEM part number; a gap that is too wide will cause misfires under load specifically because the voltage required to jump the gap exceeds the available system voltage at high RPM.

Finally, verify the fuel rail seal and intake manifold gaskets. A vacuum leak near cylinder 6 can lean out the mixture specifically for that cylinder, triggering a misfire. The behavior of the car improving after sitting suggests that fuel pressure might be dropping or that a heat soak is affecting a sensor or wire insulation. Check the oxygen sensor downstream as well; a failing O2 sensor can sometimes throw off the air-fuel ratio calculation, but it rarely causes a strict P0306 unless the mixture is so skewed it mimics a misfire.

Before tearing into the engine block, inspect the wiring harness routing near the cylinder 6 coil tower. Heat and vibration from the headers often degrade the insulation on nearby wires, causing intermittent shorts that only manifest when the engine reaches operating temperature.
